quote: I’ll label this the fallacy of privileging the hypothesis. (Do let me know if it already has an official name—I can’t recall seeing it described.)
content: It has several. In the legal setting the essay chooses, the error of considering a suspect without accounting for how they came to attention is the “prosecutor’s fallacy” family and the “island problem” of forensic statistics, in which the prior probability of a randomly selected inhabitant is what a match must be weighed against (Thompson & Schumann (1987); Balding and Donnelly, 1994, on the island problem). In statistics the general form is the multiple-comparisons or “garden of forking paths” problem: a hypothesis selected after looking cannot be evaluated as if it had been specified in advance. In philosophy of science it is the requirement that a hypothesis have a non-negligible prior before evidence can raise it, which is the Bayesian reading of the old-evidence and ad hoc debates. The essay’s formulation is a good one and its detective example is memorable. The claim to have named a fallacy the literature had not described is the claim this book makes most often, and it is usually, as here, the result of not having looked.

quote: During my recent diavlog with Scott Aaronson on quantum mechanics, I did manage to corner Scott to the extent of getting Scott to admit that there was no concrete evidence whatsoever that favors a collapse postulate or single-world quantum mechanics.
content: The identification of “single-world quantum mechanics” with “a collapse postulate” is where the argument goes wrong, and Aaronson’s own subsequent writing makes the point. Pilot-wave theory is single-world and has no collapse; it is deterministic, has none of the properties on the essay’s list except nonlocality, and reproduces the Born statistics from an equilibrium hypothesis (Valentini’s work on quantum non-equilibrium makes that hypothesis itself testable in principle). The “trillion better ways to answer the Born question” exist, and one of them was published in 1952. Aaronson’s stated position, before and after the conversation, was not that single-world theories are unsupported but that the Everett picture leaves unanswered what it is like to be a branch, how to count branches, and why the Born weights are the ones to care about, and that these are reasons for agnosticism rather than for a verdict; “cornered” is the essay’s word. The rule the essay proposes, that a hypothesis with no evidence in its favour should not be raised to attention, cuts against the hypothesis it prefers as well: there is no evidence for the existence of other branches beyond the evidence for unitarity, and whether unitarity entails branches is the interpretive question that Decoherence Is Falsifiable and Testable assumed away.

quote: Someone who spends all day thinking about whether the Trinity does or does not exist, rather than Allah or Thor or the Flying Spaghetti Monster, is more than halfway to Christianity. If leaving, they’re less than half departed; if arriving, they’re more than halfway there.
content: The psychology here is right and has an evidence base the essay does not cite. Repeated exposure to a claim raises its rated truth, the illusory-truth effect, and the effect holds even for statements the participant knows to be false (Fazio et al. (2015)); mere consideration of a hypothesis raises its subjective probability (the “explanation effect,” Ross, Lepper, Strack & Steinmetz (1977)); and attention allocated to one option among many is the mechanism by which choice-set effects operate. So “attention without evidence is more than halfway to belief without evidence” is supported. The essay’s application is the part to watch: the same mechanism operates on a reader who has spent fourteen essays considering many-worlds against one alternative, and the annotation above records which alternative was never brought to attention.
